newsitem.title: USA: Mexico hopes to prepay loans from U.S. Treasury.
newsitem.headline: Mexico hopes to prepay loans from U.S. Treasury.

text.p: Mexico hopes to pay back to the United States ahead of time more of the funds it borrowed to stem its 1995 financial meltdown, the head of the Mexican central bank said on Saturday.

Miguel Mancera, governor of the Bank of Mexico, said his country intended to repay the U.S. Treasury Department and the International Monetary Fund ahead of schedule for loans that were part of a nearly $40-billion rescue package.
"It is something that is likely," Mancera told reporters. "I cannot give you a specific date or amount, but it is something that we would like to do if possible."
In July, Mexico gave Washington a check for $7 billion, cutting to $3.5 billion its outstanding debt to the U.S. Treasury.
The Clinton administration, which patched together the international loan bailout after Congress balked at ponying up the funds, welcomed the July payment and said that Mexico was on the right track.

The crisis in Mexico began in December 1994 when the government botched an attempt to devalue its peso and sparked international investor panic that sent Mexican stock and bond markets plummeting and sapped international reserves.
With the help of the U.S.-sponsored bailout, Mexico has recovered from its worst recession in decades, and the peso has displayed remarkable strength through 1996.

Mancera, in Washington for the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings, said the peso's recent strength was due to market forces and that the government has not intervened this year to support its currency.

"We are in a floating exchange rate regime so the exchange rate is market-determined," Mancera said. "We have not intervened the whole year, except since August in order to buy dollars acording to a programme that we announced."
In August, Mexico implemented a programme to build dollar reserves that would not affect the market value of the peso.
Mancera said that international reserves, which dropped to dangerously low levels before the rescue package, were sufficient at $15.5 billion to meet Mexico's debt requirements and imports.

Mexican reserves have grown by about $4 billion because of government borrowings abroad and revenues from the state oil company Pemex, which have increased as the price of oil has risen, Mancera said.
At the height of the peso crisis, policymakers had worried that, with reserves steadily falling, the country did not have cash to repay its obligations without a rescue plan.

The Mexican economy has shown signs of improvement in recent months, and Mancera predicted better days ahead, forecasting the economy to grow by four to five percent next year and inflation easing to about half 1996 levels.
